questions.q: According to the chapter, what is the primary identity of the protagonist (the Indian artist) in the folk tradition — an individual genius or a community representative? Answer in one sentence.
questions.a: The primary identity is a community representative: the folk artist creates as part of collective rituals (e.g., women painting kohbar for weddings, tribal dances for harvest) and does not seek individual fame. A wrong answer ("individual genius") reveals the student is imposing Western Romantic notions of the artist onto a text that explicitly states "yksd dykvksa dk laca/ yksd ;k lewg ls gh Fkk" (folk arts were connected to the community).

questions.q: Apply the concept of "protagonist as tradition-bearer" to a new context: A contemporary Warli painter in Maharashtra sells canvas paintings to urban galleries. Based on the chapter's framework, identify two traits of the traditional protagonist they retain and two they must adapt. Write as four bullet points.
questions.a: Retained: (1) Uses traditional motifs (circle, triangle, square) rooted in ritual symbolism; (2) Learns through guru-shishya parampara within family. Adapted: (1) Creates for individual buyers/galleries instead of community walls; (2) Signs work with individual name instead of remaining anonymous.
